nameStory: The milky conecap gets its name from its distinctive pale, milky-white color and pointed, cone-shaped cap that resembles a tiny dunce cap. Some folks also call it the 'white dunce cap' because of this resembling a small pointed hat sitting in the grass.
description: The milky conecap is a delicate, small white mushroom that pops up in grassy areas throughout New England. This slender fungus has a distinctive cone-shaped cap that's pale white to cream-colored, sitting atop a thin, fragile stem. It's quite small and delicate, easily overlooked among the grass where it typically grows. Like other members of the conecap family, it appears quickly after rain and can disappear just as fast.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Small, cone-shaped cap that's milky white to pale cream, often with a pointed tip that gives it a distinctive dunce cap appearance

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Thin, fragile white stem that feels delicate and hollow, easily broken when handled

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: Light-colored gills that turn rusty brown as spores mature, creating a color contrast against the white cap

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Always found growing directly from grass or grassy soil, never on wood or other substrates

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: Produces a rusty brown spore print, which distinguishes it from white-spored mushrooms

habitat: Look for milky conecaps in short grass areas throughout New England, including lawns, parks, golf courses, and grassy meadows. They're saprophytic fungi that feed on decaying organic matter in the soil, often appearing in areas with rich, moist earth. You'll typically find them growing directly from the ground among grass blades rather than in wooded areas.

seasonality.spring: Begin appearing in late spring as soil warms and moisture increases, often after spring rains in grassy areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for fruiting, especially common after summer thunderstorms when they can appear almost overnight in lawns and meadows.
seasonality.fall: Continue fruiting into early fall during wet periods, though less abundantly than summer months.
seasonality.winter: Absent during winter months in New England's freezing temperatures.

funFact: Milky conecaps can appear and disappear so quickly that mycologists call them 'LBMs' - Little Brown Mushrooms (even though they're white!) - because they're ephemeral and pop up overnight after rain, sometimes lasting only a day or two before dissolving away.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other small white mushrooms in grass, but the distinctive cone shape and rusty spore print help separate it from white-spored species. Remember: 'Cone cap, rusty spores' - if it's cone-shaped but has white spores, it's something else entirely.
contextualKnowledge: This species has gone through several name changes over the years and was previously called Conocybe lactea or Conocybe albipes in older field guides, so you might see these names in books or online resources.
compareHints: Distinguished from the common conecap by its pure white coloration (common conecap is more brownish), and from the furrowedfoot conecap by its smooth stem base rather than the grooved or furrowed stem base that gives that species its name. The milky conecap is generally paler and more delicate-looking than its relatives in the genus.
